utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, would you tell us the number of this case, and be sure that the accused is present here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-10-T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would like to have the representatives of the two parties, please. Good morning, of course, to the interpreters. I assume that they can hear me. Good morning. First of all, good morning to Prosecution counsel. Perhaps you could give us the appearances, even though we know who you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Geoffrey Nice and Vladimir Tochilovsky for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Counsel for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) For the accused, Your Honours, Veselin Londrovic and my learned colleague, Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All right. Good morning to the accused as well who is now in the courtroom. We are meeting today in our public Status Conference to discuss the schedule for the Jelisic case in the light of certain events, including the fact that Judge Riad is not available, and also to set up a schedule. We can begin our discussion immediately. I have provided a draft order in which we thought that it might be good in order to deal with several of the events which have affected the composition of this Trial Chamber and which would allow us -- which is the very essence of standards in international justice, that is, to have as rapid and as equitable a trial as possible, at least as rapid as possible, if nothing else, that is, to work in such a way that we can speed the proceedings up. This is in the interests of the accused, and beyond the accused's interests, there is also the very interest of the transparency and the credibility of our international institution, and I am convinced that both the Prosecution and the Defence adhere to those principles. Having said this, and before we make any decisions, we decided, as we ordinarily do, to discuss matters with you before we take any decisions and, moreover, we will take that decision in a more direct way. All right. Since we have noted that there has been an objection on the part of the Defence which it will explain and about which we will reflect after having heard the comments from the Prosecution. The schedule would be -- what will it look like? Mr. Fourmy, can you tell us what the schedule will look like? We spoke about it, but since this is a public discussion, the schedule will be reconstructed so that it will split our proceedings because, as we know, the accused pleaded guilty to all the charges except for genocide. The initial indictment included all the charges, and then there is the sentencing aspect which will become -- or joint, rather, that is, for the genocide and for the other charges. In a draft order, we gave the reasons why we might split the case into two parts. Let me give the floor to the Legal Officer of the Trial Chamber so that he can explain what we are talking about in respect of economy of our work. Mr. Fourmy, would you like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour. In fact, in the scheduling order dated 12 March, 1999, the Trial Chamber expressed the desire to hold a Status Conference so that we can discuss the appropriateness of taking a decision in respect of those charges to which Goran Jelisic pleaded guilty further to the agreement which was made between the Prosecution and the Defence and which deals with almost all of the charges originally brought against Mr. Jelisic, subject to several modifications and except for the important distinction of genocide to which the accused pleaded not guilty. During the further initial appearance of 29 October, the question was quickly raised and discussed, that is, to know how the review of the case would be handled insofar as, theoretically, according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, when an accused pleads guilty, the Trial Chamber requests that the registry set a hearing date in order to rule on the penalty. Given the fact that there were two parts, there was one to which the accused pleaded guilty and the other part to which he pleaded not guilty, after having heard the parties, the Trial Chamber noted that it would not rule even in respect of the guilt of the accused as regards the guilty plea and, therefore, even less so on any possible penalty that would be handed down and postponing that until the end of the proceedings in respect of the crime of genocide. The suggestion was agreed to by both parties, and under these conditions, the trial for genocide was supposed to begin in December, and since Judge Riad, for medical reasons, was not able to be present at the trial and because he is still away -- and we do hope that he will be able to resume his work with the Judges at this Tribunal around the beginning of May 1999 -- under these conditions, the Trial Chamber wanted to hold this Status Conference in order to review once again the situation and to discuss with the parties in respect of the appropriateness of making separate decisions, that is, separate -- the plea, insofar as Goran Jelisic would have the opportunity to know what penalty, according to the Trial Chamber and in respect of proof brought by the parties, would be handed down. This has not yet been decided because there has been no decision from the Trial Chamber yet, that is, at the time that this order of 12 March was prepared, but the idea would be that we would take advantage as soon as possible after Judge Riad's return, that is, something would happen during the month of May so that we might be able to have a decision possibly, should that be the direction that the decision is going to take in respect to the work, that is, a decision on the guilty pleas in June, which would then allow, once again, the accused Goran Jelisic to have a very clear idea of what the Trial Chamber's position is in respect of those crimes to which he pleaded guilty. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) And I thank you. Perhaps we could first hear what the Prosecutor has to say and then, of course, we would hear what the Defence wants to say because we know that the Defence objects to this idea. Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to the Trial Chamber moving to sentencing in respect of the guilty pleas but recognises at the moment that there are Defence objections. Of course, we have yet to hear in any detail those objections. Whatever the decision may be about sentencing on the guilty pleas, the Prosecution would invite the Chamber, now or in due course, to complete the process that was started by the guilty pleas by making a pronouncement of guilt in accordance with Rule 62, and I understand that that invitation or proposal by me may be non-controversial; it may be something to which the Defence will offer no objection. At the moment, I think that is all I can help with, save to say that the Prosecution's concern -- and I think this is a concern shared by everyone -- is that the maximum priority should be given to the speedy determination of the genocide issue that is important and is outstanding. I have raised informally and only very recently another proposal whereby the difficulties, the timetable difficulties, that the Chamber is facing, might be reduced or overcome, but perhaps now isn't the moment to mention that publicly. I will wait and see what else develops in the course of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All right. You can do it later in the morning. Perhaps we will hear what Judge -- but before we hear the Prosecution's new suggestion, we might first listen to what the Defence has to say, that is, the draft memorandum for setting up a calendar. Mr. Greaves, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour, there are a number of matters I want to raise concerning the issue of sentencing that is now being proposed by Your Honour. The first objection that we have is that the Trial Chamber, as presently composed, being only of two Judges, does not have jurisdiction to set a date for sentencing. Can I refer Your Honour to the two Rules which deal with the issue of sentence? In the first instance, Rule 62(vi) says this: "The Trial Chamber shall, in the case of a plea of guilty act in accordance with Rule 62 bis." The phraseology of that Rule is effectively mandatory. It is not a discretionary rule, it requires Your Honour to act, in the case of a guilty plea, in the case of Rule 62 bis. Looking at Rule 62 bis, that sets out what should happen in respect of a guilty plea, and it's the final part of that order that says this: "The Trial Chamber may enter a finding of guilt and instruct the registrar to set a date for the sentencing hearing." I stress the words "Trial Chamber," because it is our position that that can only be a fully composed, three-Judge bench which can set a date for a sentencing hearing. We make the second observation that it is not a mandatory rule but a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) On this point, let me stop you right now so we don't waste any time. It was never a question for the Trial Chamber to rule on the sentencing with only two Judges. There's no point, perhaps, in even wasting our time about that, because it is absolutely clear, and I think the purpose of today's discussion is not to know whether Judge Rodrigues and Judge Riad are going to rule on the fate of Mr. Jelisic, it's self-evident this could only be made once Judge Riad has returned, and that even the statement in respect of jurisdiction, the last sentence of 62 bis will be taken with two Judges. Therefore, let's try to speed things forward. So the first objection, I can tell you immediately, is that we agree with you, because that's the interpretation of the text which is perfectly clear and perfectly readable. The second objection, please move to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's most helpful, Your Honour. We have a number of objections on the merits of proceeding to sentence in respect of the matters to which he's pleaded guilty for the conclusion for trial in respect of genocide. At his trial for genocide we intend to call witnesses. Some of those deal only with issues of fact, others deal only with issues relating to sentence. The majority, however, are witnesses we intend should give evidence both as to matters of fact and as to matters of mitigation of sentence. It is concerning that latter group that we are most anxious. There are two reasons for this. The first is this: If a hearing in respect of sentence is held, a witness who is relevant both as to sentence and as to issues of fact will, therefore, be forced to give evidence on two occasions, at a sentencing hearing and again during the trial. There is already considerable anxiety on the part of witnesses about having to attend the Tribunal. Your Honours are fully familiar with the concerns of all people in the former Yugoslavia about the potential repercussions of giving evidence before the Tribunal and it is a realistic and live problem. It is perhaps even more so in the area of Brcko, which the events of the genocide trial concern, because of the high tensions that continue to exist there, particularly in the light of recent decisions made in respect of the future status of that municipality. Some witnesses, who it is proposed to call, are members of one community and some are from another. Many Serbian witnesses have to work in the Federation. There are very real concerns about giving evidence. We fear, and we believe this to be a realistic fear, that it will prove impossible to get witnesses to give evidence twice before this tribunal. If just one witness were to be deterred from giving evidence, both as to sentence and as to issues of fact, that would be a significant matter of prejudice to the accused. The second matter is this: Witnesses are likely to give evidence about matters which are factual matters, but which have a relevance both to sentence and as to fact. In other words, a witness may give evidence at a sentencing hearing about some set of facts which are relevant both to mitigation and as to issues of guilt or innocence. The affect of holding a sentencing hearing at which such evidence is given would enable the Prosecution to hear Defence evidence on fact before its own case has closed. That, we submit, is not in accordance with the Rules and would also have the effect of giving the Prosecution a significant and unfair advantage if it were able to hear the Defence case or part of the Defence case before its own case were closed. We submit that either of those factors, taken on its own, strongly mitigates against the proposed course which is suggested. Taken together, we submit that they are very strong reasons not to proceed to the issue of sentencing. The next matter is this: The offences to which he's pleaded guilty already form, as we understand the Prosecution's case, a significant part of their case on genocide. Witnesses for the Prosecution are likely to give evidence about those matters, and it is possible that some of that evidence may yet assist the defendant on mitigation. If he's already been sentenced in respect of the murders to which he's pleaded guilty, he would not have the benefit of evidence given at the trial in mitigation of sentence. We submit that that is yet another potential unfairness. The next matter is this: The offences, as I've pointed out, to which he's pleaded guilty, form part of the basis upon which the Prosecution say he is also guilty of genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me for a moment, please. I'm not sure I understood your last objection. You're saying that the accused could plead guilty if there were mitigating circumstances, it would not be to his advantage. I haven't followed exactly what you said. I didn't really understand you. Could you go back again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let me explain it again. The Prosecution intends to call further witnesses, and as presently suggested, that would be after he has been sentenced in respect of the matters to which he's pleaded guilty. It is possible that such witnesses may, during the course of their evidence, give evidence which is or assists to mitigate the defendant's guilt in respect of those matters to which he's pleaded guilty. If he has already been sentenced by the time that evidence was given, he is effectively going to be deprived of the assistance of that evidence because it comes after the sentencing hearing. We submit that if he's deprived of the potential for that, it creates a potential unfairness to him. I hope I've explained better on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, yes. I'm sure I should have paid closer attention. Excuse me, Mr. Greaves. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was then going on to say this: As I have explained, the matters to which he's pleaded guilty form part of the Prosecution's case on genocide. We would respectfully submit that it is illogical and artificial to try and separate those matters, the one from another. They essentially go together and try and sentence him piecemeal in respect of one aspect of what the Prosecution say is genocide, and that, of course, depends on him being convicted of genocide, is illogical and we would respectfully submit that it is a proper principle of sentencing that an accused should be sentenced only on one occasion in respect of all his crimes, particularly where there is such a close relationship between the matters to which he's pleaded guilty and upon the matter which he may yet be convicted. We are, of course, conscious of the importance of the expeditious trial provisions that exist in both the Statute and Rules; they are important. However, their principle purpose is this, if I may say so: They exist to ensure that if somebody is detained and has pleaded not guilty, that his trial takes place speedily, and if he's acquitted, that he is released speedily. There is some distinction to be drawn between that situation and the situation of this accused. He has pleaded guilty to matters which on any sensible and rational view will attract a substantial sentence, and he is going to be remaining in custody well beyond the period in which any trial could be concluded. So the principle purpose for which the fair trial, expeditious trial provisions exist, have a rather less practical application to his situation. He's going to be staying here, the trial will take place, and will be completed well within the time of any sentence that he has to serve in respect to the guilty pleas. Our final concerns are these: The defendant is very much focused on the issue of his trial for genocide, and as counsel we have to spend a lot of time with him, assisting him to focus on those issues. We are extremely concerned that to raise now the issue of sentence will, in fact, particularly in the circumstances I've outlined, have a debilitating effect on the defendant's present condition. He will forgive me for saying this in public, he does suffer at times from a considerable degree of stress, and as it may be known, he is under constant surveillance within the prison concerning his condition. We are extremely anxious that the process of sentencing will distract him very considerably from the issue of his trial, and bring about a deterioration in his condition. That, we submit, is something which the Trial Chamber should, at all costs, avoid. It would be most undesirable if that was brought about. It makes the task of all of us much harder if the defendant is in an unstable condition. For all those reasons, we respectfully submit that it is not appropriate, at the present time, to proceed to the issue of sentencing, that it would, in fact, be more appropriate if he's convicted of genocide, to deal with all matters in one single go than to deal with matters in a piecemeal and haphazard fashion. My leading counsel, Mr. Londrovic, also wishes to raise with Your Honours what the former Yugoslavian sentencing practice was in relation to sentencing people in a piecemeal fashion because, of course, Your Honour, I think, has to consider the issue of the practice and procedure of the former Yugoslavia when considering sentencing. I would now like to pass the floor to him, if I may with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, bearing in mind the provisions of the Statute of the International Court which states that the court will bear in mind the sentencing according to Yugoslav criminal law, and as far as Yugoslav criminal law is concerned, it is regulated in the Law on Criminal Procedure which is a federal law, which after the disintegration of Yugoslavia was taken over by the Republika Srpska, that is to say, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and bearing in mind the Dayton agreements and peace accords, it is in force throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina at present. It is regulated by Article 348.2, which states, "If the indictment encompasses a number of criminal acts, in just one sentence it will be stated whether and for what crime the indictment is pronounced guilty or is freed of the guilt." So in a situation where the indictment contains a number of criminal acts, it is up to the court to bring in just one sentence, and that one sentence, depending on the evidence provided, it can theoretically be -- it can find the accused guilty or not guilty or whatever, but there is just one sentencing. Under Yugoslav criminal procedure there is no possibility of bringing in two sentences on the basis of one indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Londrovic. Before we give the floor back to the Prosecutor, I would like to say that the first objection we do not accept. We overrule that objection. The second objection could be overcome. I'm making suggestions of course, I'm just reviewing your objections. The second objection, it's difficult for the witness to resolve those difficulties, once he comes here for his sentencing, we could keep him and hear what he has to say about genocide. The third objection, and we'll hear what -- well, according to the third objection the Prosecution would have allegedly some advantage in hearing certain testimony before -- well, let me hear -- I'll wait for Mr. Nice to make some comments about this. The fourth objection regarding elements that have already been renounced, that is mitigating circumstances, this is an objection which I asked you to repeat, but ordinarily I think the Prosecution has the obligation already to provide you with all exculpatory materials. Therefore, I don't think this is really a valid objection. I recognise as much more valid the fifth objection, when you say there is a separation in your mind which appears artificial. The sixth objection, in my opinion, is not valid. Rather, to the contrary. I would say that if the accused is really interested in his sentence, the objection would be that the client is not really available to concentrate on genocide because he's going to be focused on the sentence. I think that that's an argument which could be turned around and turned back against your objection, because in the end one could say the opposite, that is, one could say no, to the contrary, Mr. Jelisic might be focused on his sentence, but he could also, with all the time in the world before him and all the time that you have with him, he could then focus on his trial for genocide. Therefore, looking at the matter the other way. The seventh objection I also find significant, however, in fact, yes, is the psychological condition of the accused. Lastly, Mr. Fourmy has given me a counter-objection to what I said about hearing witnesses at the same time. Yes, those would be Defence witnesses, and we could not perhaps hear them immediately. I do acknowledge that that objection is valid. All right. I throw this out to you. There are seven objections that you have raised. I have counted seven here. Some, in my opinion, can be gotten around and others which do merit discussion. I would like to turn to Mr. Jelisic, because it is your trial, Mr. Jelisic, and independently, of course, of any confidence that you have in your attorneys, both of the Judges would like to hear what you have to say. First of all, do you understand what is at stake here and what the concern of the Judges is, that is, a concern which is one of having expediency and to be sure that you know what is going to happen to you after having pleaded guilty to the charges, and there are other problems -- I can also point this out to Mr. Greaves -- there are other problems; for example, where will the sentence be served? What is he going to do? We are not making any arbitrary kinds of decisions here, but I would like to tell you, Mr. Greaves, that contrary to what you may have thought, the Trial Chamber was not struck all of a sudden by a kind of legal whim according to which it would have put aside its intelligence and its foresight or its legal understanding. You are dealing with professional Judges, let me remind you, and it is as professionals that we studied all the conditions under which this Jelisic trial could be held. Mr. Jelisic, what do you think? You. I am speaking about you personally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, my personal opinion is that I support the proposal made by my lawyers and that we continue the trial for genocide because there has been a great deal of problems in bringing witnesses twice here for the reasons we all know. In view of the fact that I am under supervision and my state of health -- I don't want you to misunderstand me, but I don't think that there will be another sentence brought in -- I don't want to be in a position where there will be no sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Tell us about your health. Speak to us a little bit about your detention conditions, about your health. First, speak to us about your mental condition, if you want to -- how do you feel now? You don't have to go into all the details. If you prefer to be seated, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I did not hear the question, I'm sorry. I wasn't getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I was asking you what your health is, how is your health, how do you feel, and I was saying that if you prefer to sit down in order to answer, you may sit down. Have you heard what I said now? Has it been interpreted? Do you hear me, Mr. Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) If you prefer to be seated, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) There's no need. I will remain standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) How do you feel? Are you tired? How is your detention going? Are you getting medical attention? Are people taking care of you properly? I hope they are. Would you explain it to us? Tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, all my problems are being very successfully treated by the warden of the detention unit, Mr. McFadden. I said that I did not take therapy yesterday until I learnt about this, that is to say, what is going to be the subject of discussion. Perhaps this is not the time or place for me to disclose what I have in my defence, but I think that, as my attorney has said, it will be a historical trial -- I think it will be a little bit more than historical when I present my defence and my evidence because I know that there is a very ugly picture of me here, an ugly image, but there is quite another picture that I am going to present, and so I am not going to say that here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All right. Thank you. Judge Rodrigues, you want to ask some questions? Thank you. You may be seated, Mr. Jelisic. All right. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have understood that there were six or seven objections raised by the Defence that the accused -- and with all of these, there are some objections that are stronger than others, but I forgot to speak about what Mr. Londrovic said. Yes, of course, the practice of the former Yugoslavia is, of course, our reference, but we also have a Rule in our Rules which says that we ourselves have to give a sentence for each of the charges or each of the counts. Is that true, Mr. Fourmy?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, yes, that is the practice which has been held up to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, this is a practice which could be challenged, of course, let me point that out to you, that it is not, in and of itself, absurd to think that we might have two sentences and then bring them together later on. Turning to the Prosecution, do you have any responses to what the Defence has said and perhaps some proposals, suggestions, which we hope will be constructive ones? Mr. Nice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) ... Interpretation. Just a moment, please. I'm not getting interpretation. I hear you speaking, but I would like to hear the interpretation. Is it working now? All right. Let's try. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will repeat what I was saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I hear you. Yes, all right. Now, proceed please. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have nothing to say about the defendant's state of health save respectfully to suggest you may wish to be sure you understand from his own counsel what lay behind his observation about there being no second sentence if that part of his own address was other than clear to you. I believe that his counsel will be able to assist you with an interpretation of that. As to the arguments that have been raised by my two learned friends, there is, of course, some logic in some or all of those arguments, but the potential for logic has to be seen beside the weight to be attached to each of those arguments. So, for example, the difficulty of getting witnesses here twice is something that will be recognised, I think, by this Tribunal, for it is something that is referred to not only by Defence, when they have witnesses to call, but also by the Prosecution. What I can't help you with, because it is a matter known only to my learned friends, is the number of witnesses that that would involve and what material, if any, they have to show that there would be a real risk with those particular witnesses that the witnesses would not attend. I can see a way to weighing or evaluating, in quantum terms, that objection. The method might be for the Defence to have, on this occasion, some ex parte access to the Court to identify the witnesses and the particular problems, but that will be a matter both for them to decide to seek such access and then for the Court to grant it. So far as the objection that the Prosecution would hear the Defence case in advance, it may be that that is only a slight risk, if risk at all, for evidence on mitigation can be narrowly confined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Are you talking about an ex parte hearing, but for what purpose? I didn't understand that, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because the Defence say that they would have a difficulty calling witnesses twice and because I can't deal with that in quantum terms, in quantity terms -- I don't know how many witnesses and I don't know to what extent any particular witness is fragile or has already expressed anxiety about attending twice -- I can't help further. But it may be, if the Defence sought an ex parte hearing and if the Chamber granted one, that they would be able more openly to explain the particular risks or problems with calling witnesses that they perceive. I hope that makes that clear. Dealing then with the next point, the problem of the Defence case being heard in advance, evidence in mitigation should, it may be thought, be capable of being closely confined, and there would be, of course, be no right to cross-examine beyond the substance of the evidence, bearing in mind the purpose for which it was being led, and it may be that that objection is one that in real terms has little weight. The potential for Prosecution witnesses to assist in mitigation, I can understand why it is raised, and it seems to me, yes, there is a theoretical possibility that that is a good ground of objection. The witness whose witness statement paints a black picture but who, in cross-examination, or indeed simply of his own volition, says one or more things favourable to the accused, would be giving evidence that might affect the picture at the time of sentencing. At present, we are not aware of any possibility, let alone probability, that the witnesses we propose to call would be likely to give any such evidence, so again, although it is logically a possible ground for objection, the Chamber might decide that it is an objection that, in fact, has little weight. The illogicality of separating sentence for some crimes from the sentence for other crimes part of the same course of conduct is something that Your Honour has recognised and that I think systems around the world tend to recognise, and it may be that in the absence of good and compelling reason, it is prudent to sentence a defendant on a single occasion for all the matters to which he falls for sentence, whether by plea of guilty or otherwise. So far as Mr. Londrovic's point is concerned -- and he will correct me on this, of course, if I am wrong -- I understand that there is at least this distinction between the system in the former Yugoslavia and the system for this Tribunal, namely, that in the former Yugoslavia, there was never the potential for moving directly from a plea of guilty to sentence because even where a defendant pleaded guilty -- and I hope I'm right in this -- there was nevertheless a full trial. So that a Trial Chamber would always be seized of the whole case or dossier, and one can understand why there would be simply formally no potential for separate sentencing in respect of separate counts. I think I'm right in that, and I am very grateful for Mr. Tochilovsky for his wider knowledge of the practice in the former Yugoslavia than I myself have. The consent of a defendant to deferment of sentencing in his case may be thought to cure problems which understandably concern the Trial Chamber because one well recognises that the pressure of work on the Chamber is bringing difficulties not, of course, of its creation, and that it is anxious, wherever possible, to move to conclusions; but, as I say, consent of the defendant himself may go some way to allaying those concerns and curing the problem but if and only if, in our respectful submission at this stage, first the Chamber moves toward that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- sorry, moves towards that decision allowed for in 62 bis, namely, the finding of guilt, and there has been no objection raised by my learned friends to that step being taken in an appropriate way and providing, of course, that the Chamber has in mind, as it knows it does, the proper interest in a speedy trial. I don't know if I can assist further. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Greaves, excuse me. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I just wanted to deal with two matters that were raised by my friend. As to the formal entering of verdicts of guilty, neither my learned friend Mr. Londrovic nor I, I anticipate, would have any objection to the formality of that being done, unless the defendant has any particular objection, and I'm sorry not to have dealt with that earlier. I apologise. My learned friend also raised a query as to what was precisely meant by the defendant's observation. I think what was meant and I stand to be corrected by my client, that when he said there is no need for a second sentence, that he was anticipating that if he was acquitted for the offence of genocide then there would be no second sentencing hearing in the circumstances that are now being proposed. But as I understood what he was saying, was he thankfully supporting his counsel in their observations about this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, maybe we should ask him what he meant, because to tell you the truth, I don't understand. I'm completely lost. All right. The accused is here and both of us Judges would like to ask the accused, pursuant to our rules, ask the accused what he meant when he said there wouldn't be a second sentence. If you would please explain what you meant Mr. Jelisic, if you want to. If you don't want to, it doesn't matter, then don't, but I don't want to make an exegesis of your thoughts, since you are the person most concerned by all of this. All right. Mr. Jelisic, what did you mean when you said there would not be a second sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Perhaps my counsel did not understand me and they may have expected a different answer, but I had had something else in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, Your Honours. I understood my client perfectly well, and I think if you want to hear the answer to this question we should lower the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You're correct. Absolutely. We'll go into a closed session. Just a moment, please, Mr. Jelisic. Let me remind Mr. Jelisic that if he does not want to respond, he does not have to. I simply do not -- well, since we're talking about Mr. Jelisic's mind, this is a Status Conference, and he was asked about his health and his detention conditions. I don't accept his having said something that I don't understand. Therefore, I would like things to be very, very clear and it will be private session. We don't have to go into a closed session, private session will be sufficient, as long as it takes for Mr. Jelisic to explain what he means. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'll give the floor back to Mr. Greaves if he has anything further to say, because we were now at the second point. After that, I think, we will be able to close the session. Mr. Greaves, we can move back into a public session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have nothing to add. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Judge Rodrigues? No, he has nothing to add. Mr. Londrovic, do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I have nothing further to add. I'm convinced that the Chamber will adopt the best decision, that it will consider the need of a fair trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Let me turn to Mr. Fourmy to ask whether there are any other suggestions or any other comments. Perhaps the Prosecutor has something to state, Mr. President. Mr. Nice, would you care to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have one proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, you've got proposals. I thought that you had given up the idea of making constructive proposals, but you said that you would make proposals. Yes, it's true, you did say that. All right. I'm opening my notebook again and I am all ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My proposal relates to the timetable difficulties faced by the Chamber, of which we are all aware, and the proposal for consideration is that evidence might, in this case, be taken by way of deposition. The timetable problems constituting the special circumstances will be required to justify the taking of depositions. I go a little further with my proposal, hoping not to be thought to be presumptuous in doing so, and observe that Judge Riad, on his return to health and to the Tribunal, just may, and of course we can't know the answer to this, may have time available. There may, of course, be a courtroom in this building available, and the taking of evidence by deposition not only would speed the process to trial but would also meet some of the witness difficulties that both sides may face, in particular, those difficulties of timetabling witnesses, for were there to be a programme of deposition taking in a courtroom that was otherwise free, then witnesses could be brought according to a fairly gentle programme, and there should be neither pressure of time on the witness, the advocates, nor were it to be Judge Riad, the Judge taking the deposition. Depositions, can, of course, with the machinery available in these courts, be taken in such a way that at closing argument, counsel on one side or another could replay, as if live, relevant passages of the evidence. That's the proposal that I had in mind. I only had an opportunity to mention it very briefly to Mr. Greaves this morning, because I know that he's been out of the country right up until last night, and, indeed, I didn't take the opportunity of mentioning it to Mr. Fourmy until yesterday. That is a specific proposal to deal with timetable problems, and if it finds favour or if it may find favour, we'll draft the appropriate motion which should really support such procedure. There's a second discreet procedural matter that I'd like to mention now, although it won't take very long, and it concerns the extended interviews of the defendant with an investigator. Those interviews exist, at the moment, in their original language and in translation into English, and I do not believe at present they exist in the French form. In cases like this, where what is at stake is the state of mine of an accused, it is typically the case that each side will regard substantial passages of those interviews as of value to the finder of fact. In some jurisdictions, either the whole interview will be played as a tape recording, or extensive passages will be read out to the court, sometimes with an advocate taking one role, perhaps the role of the investigator, and an investigator, as witness, taking the role of the accused, or some such system. That plainly cannot happen in this Tribunal where we have to work in two languages, and where, as we recognise, it is the misfortune of the presiding Judge not to have the advantages that the English practitioners have of LiveNote. Therefore, it presents a practical problem for resolution, and a resolution that we know should be one that is economic in the use of time. I've discussed this with Mr. Fourmy, and one proposal that he's raised which seems sensible, although again I've only been able to mention it briefly to Mr. Greaves, is that if the parties, that is, Prosecution and Defence, were to identify within the overall transcript the passages each would want read, then we can ensure in good time that those passages are translated into the appropriate languages, and if the court accepted this as a practice, we could then invite the court to read those documents in an appropriate language, making such limited points in live evidence as would be appropriate. I should say that the interviews occupy a full lever-arch binder, as at present constituted. One would hope, of course, that large passages would not have to be read, if they're just background and matters that don't touch on the defendant's state of mind. Those are the only two specific proposals that I wanted to mention now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Mr. Greaves? Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as those two suggestions are concerned, my friend is right. We and I had only very briefly discussed them before Your Honours came in. I have not had an opportunity to discuss them with my leading counsel and, in turn, we have not had an opportunity to discuss them with the accused, and I would really like not to be asked to comment any further at this present stage, please. You can understand that I'm not in a position to give a definitive answer on our behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, I understand. The difficulty in respect of depositions is the following: You're referring to Rule 71, I suppose; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The difficulty is that Rule 71 that we have already used in this Trial Chamber when one of the Judges was unable to be with us, and that was, of course, with the agreement of the accused, it was done with the agreement of the accused, in this Trial Chamber we have a very exponential interpretation of this Rule which was accepted by the parties, but I think the difficulty, and I think subject to anything that Mr. Fourmy or my colleague want to say, is I do not see under what exceptional circumstances could justify Judge Riad's sitting as kind of a presiding officer, whereas the two other Trial Chamber Judges would be sitting in another case. I'm not sure that that would be very transparent. What do you think, Mr. Fourmy?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I think that Mr. Nice, in advance, had both the possibility that the Trial Chamber might consider that the scheduling problems in and of themselves would constitute exceptional circumstances covered by Rule 71. Having said that, in terms of the transparency of two Trial Chambers and one Trial Chamber are sitting in a public session, whereas the third would also be somewhere else, that would be difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) What do you think, Judge Rodrigues? We're speaking very freely here. When we had a Judge who was ill, we did that, and we wanted to make it very clear that it was a specific proceeding and we wore civilian clothes. In other Trial Chambers we did wear robes, but we used Rule 71. Therefore, I am in favour of a very extended conception of this Rule but I do wonder whether a Judge -- well, if a Judge can hear depositions, that means that he's not ill. You always come up against that problem. If one of the Judges is designated as the presiding officer, that means he is capable of being a Judge full time. If he's full time, then he has to be here with us at the bench. That's what I meant. All right. I think that we can't say anything further than what we've said already. Thank you, Mr. Nice, for having tried to make a contribution to resolve the scheduling problems that the Trial Chamber is facing. Comment? All right. We are going to adjourn the hearing, unless Judge Rodrigues would like to say something. No objections? Thank you very much for coming. We close this Status Conference now and, of course, the Judges, in respect of what has been said, the useful contributions that you've made, thanks to that contributions, the Judges will be able to give you a response. All right. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: adjourned at 10.30 a.m. sine die 23 24 25
